column1: What are the four origins of style declarations in CSS, listed in increasing precedence order (before !important is considered)?
column2: User-agent stylesheets, user stylesheets, author stylesheets, and inline style attributes — each later origin overrides the earlier ones in the base cascade.

column1: How does the !important annotation invert the normal cascade order, and why is this invariant important for accessibility?
column2: !important declarations are collected into a separate shadow hierarchy where user !important overrides author !important, which overrides normal author/user rules. This guarantees user accessibility overrides can never be silently suppressed by application author styles.

column1: Why is CSS specificity modeled as a lexicographic tuple (ID, class/attribute, type) rather than a single scalar weight?
column2: Lexicographic comparison prevents lower-order components from ever outweighing higher-order ones — e.g., no number of type selectors can overflow into beating a single class selector, and no number of class selectors can beat a single ID selector.

column1: How does CSS inheritance differ semantically from object-oriented class inheritance?
column2: CSS inheritance propagates property values down the DOM tree (a HAS-A containment relationship in the visual hierarchy) when no cascaded value exists, whereas OO inheritance establishes IS-A relationships with vtable polymorphism.

column1: What are the four concentric regions of the CSS box model, from innermost to outermost?
Which box-model region belongs to no element and carries no background or pointer events?
column2: Margin — it is interpersonal space between elements that participates in layout positioning but has no visual rendering or event capture of its own.

column1: By the original CSS 2.1 specification, what do the `width` and `height` properties apply to, and what formula gives the total rendered width of an element?
column2: They apply only to the content area. Total rendered width = content-width + padding-left + padding-right + border-left + border-right (margins excluded).

column1: How does `box-sizing: border-box` redefine the meaning of `width` and `height`, and how does the browser compute the content area under this model?
column2: It redefines width/height as the outer edge of the border (not the content edge). The browser back-calculates content width as: specified-width − padding-left − padding-right − border-left − border-right.

column1: What is the fundamental dimensional distinction between Flexbox and Grid as layout algorithms?
column2: Flexbox is a one-dimensional algorithm that reasons along a single main axis (cross-axis resolved after), while Grid is a two-dimensional algorithm that defines an explicit row/column track lattice independent of content, then places items into cells.

column1: In Flexbox's layout algorithm, in what order does the browser resolve main-axis vs. cross-axis sizing?
column2: The browser first evaluates each item's hypothetical main-size, distributes free space via flex-grow/flex-shrink along the main axis, and only handles cross-axis sizing/alignment after the main-axis calculation is complete.

column1: What is the core tradeoff triangle underlying every CSS styling architecture (CSS-in-JS, utility-first, preprocessors)?
column2: Developer ergonomics, runtime performance, and build complexity — e.g., CSS-in-JS maximizes ergonomics but adds runtime overhead; utility-first frameworks shift cost to build time; preprocessors have zero runtime cost but require manual scope/specificity management.

column1: Why does encountering a `<link rel="stylesheet">` tag block render tree construction, and in what direction do browsers match CSS selectors against the DOM?
column2: Because the browser cannot resolve the specificity graph until CSSOM parsing completes, stylesheets are render-blocking. Selectors are matched right-to-left, starting from the rightmost (key) selector and traversing upward through ancestors.
